verses.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘Assign the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you by Moses,
that the man slayer who kills any person accidentally or unintentionally may flee there. They shall be to you for a refuge from the avenger of blood.

He shall flee to one of those cities, and shall stand at the entrance of the gate of the city, and declare his case in the ears of the elders of that city. They shall take him into the city with them, and give him a place, that he may live among them.
If the avenger of blood pursues him, then they shall not deliver up the man slayer into his hand; because he struck his neighbor unintentionally, and didn’t hate him before.

He shall dwell in that city until he stands before the congregation for judgment, until the death of the high priest that shall be in those days. Then the man slayer shall return, and come to his own city, and to his own house, to the city he fled from.’”
They set apart Kedesh in Galilee in the hill country of Naphtali, Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kiriath Arba (also called Hebron) in the hill country of Judah.

Beyond the Jordan at Jericho eastward, they assigned Bezer in the wilderness in the plain out of the tribe of Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead out of the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan out of the tribe of Manasseh.

These were the appointed cities for all the children of Israel, and for the alien who lives among them, that whoever kills any person unintentionally might flee there, and not die by the hand of the avenger of blood, until he stands trial before the congregation.

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks again to Joshua—not in battle, but in mercy. Even after the sword has done its work, the Kingdom of heaven still makes room for the accidentally wounded and the refugee.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cities of refuge were spoken of long before, by Moses in the wilderness. Now Joshua is to make them real in the land. The same mercy God promised at Sinai is still alive in Canaan.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There is a God-breathed difference between the killer in anger and the man struck by accident. The refuge shelters not crime but truth—a place where the law sees what the eye of vengeance cannot.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At the gate—the place of judgment and community witness—the one who fled must stand and speak his case to the elders. The refuge demands honesty and a hearing, not hiding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The avenger's rage, howling outside the gate, must stop. The city stands between hot blood and cold judgment, saying, 'Wait. He did not hate. Let righteousness, not revenge, have the final word.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Looking back from our own time, we hear an echo: the refuge holds until the high priest dies—a picture of how our own High Priest's death opened a way home for us to leave our hiding and be fully restored.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kedesh, Shechem, Kiriath Arba—three cities on the west side, scattered through the hills where the people live. Mercy was not meant to be far away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: And three more across the Jordan to the east—Bezer, Ramoth, Golan. No matter which side of the river you dwelt on, refuge was near. God's mercy stretches as wide as His land.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the alien, the stranger, may flee to these cities. In the Lord's law, justice and mercy for the accidentally broken know no border, no bloodline. All who kill unintentionally may find shelter before the judge.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
